headings.title: Introduction to Newborn Primitive Reflexes
headings.content: Primitive reflexes are involuntary, stereotypic movement patterns originating in the subcortical regions of the central nervous system. They emerge during intrauterine life and are fully present in a healthy term newborn. These automatic responses are essential for early neonatal survival, helping the infant feed, protect itself, and interact with its new environment. As the cerebral cortex matures and myelinates over the first several months of life, these primitive movements are gradually inhibited. Midwives assess these reflexes during the initial neonatal examination to verify the structural and functional integrity of the infant's central nervous system.

headings.title: Physiological Basis and Purpose of Rooting
headings.content: The rooting reflex ensures the newborn can locate a source of nourishment without conscious thought. When the cheek or the corner of the infant's mouth is stroked, sensory receptors in the skin transmit impulses via the trigeminal nerve to the brainstem. The infant responds by automatically turning the head toward the stimulus, opening the mouth, and lowering the tongue in preparation for latching. This reaction is paired closely with the sucking reflex to secure feeding. Beyond nutrition, rooting serves a protective and communicative function, helping the mother and baby establish early skin-to-skin contact and successful breastfeeding routines in the postnatal ward.

headings.title: Rooting Reflex Assessment Technique
headings.content:
To test the rooting reflex correctly, the midwife places the baby in a comfortable, quiet, and warm environment, ensuring the infant is not crying or deeply asleep. The midwife gently strokes the skin at the corner of the baby's mouth, moving outward along the cheek, or gently touching the upper or lower lip.

- **Cheek stroke**: The infant turns the head toward the side that was stroked.
- **Upper lip stroke**: The infant tilts the head backward and opens the mouth.
- **Lower lip stroke**: The infant drops the jaw and lowers the tongue to prepare for latching.

Avoid performing this assessment immediately after a heavy feed, as a satiated newborn may show a weak or absent response despite a healthy nervous system.

headings.title: Normal Findings and Age of Integration
headings.content: In a healthy term infant, the rooting reflex is robust and easily elicited on both sides of the face. Bilateral symmetry is expected; a response that appears only on one side warrants closer observation. The reflex gradually integrates—meaning it fades from conscious prominence as voluntary control takes over—around three to four months of age, though it may persist longer during sleep. Integration happens sooner when the infant is awake and alert, as voluntary head turning and visual tracking replace automatic feeding responses.

headings.title: Abnormal Responses: Hyperactive and Absent Reflexes
headings.content: Variations from the expected rooting response can signal underlying neurological distress. An absent or severely sluggish reflex on both sides may point toward central nervous system depression, severe birth asphyxia, prematurity, or systemic illness. Conversely, a hyperactive response or persistent rooting long past the expected integration age can indicate chronic neurological damage or developmental delay. Asymmetry—where one side responds briskly while the other is weak or non-responsive—often suggests local nerve injury, such as facial nerve palsy sustained during a difficult forceps or vacuum-assisted delivery.

headings.title: Implications for Midwifery Practice and Breastfeeding
headings.content: Midwives leverage the rooting reflex to support successful breastfeeding initiation during the critical golden hour after birth. Placing the naked newborn prone on the mother's chest allows the infant to use natural rooting and crawling behaviors to self-attach to the breast. Midwives should counsel mothers to watch for early feeding cues—such as head turning, mouth opening, and hand-to-mouth movements—rather than waiting for distress crying, which makes latching difficult. Recognizing normal versus abnormal reflex patterns also empowers the midwife to identify birth injuries early and refer high-risk neonates for pediatric evaluation without delay.
